planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic soil in partial shade; Jubilation is a Southern Living Plant Collection release bred for unusually large flowers on a more compact, cold-hardy plant than older gardenia cultivars.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade to morning sun with afternoon shade. Jubilation is a Southern Living Plant Collection gardenia bred for exceptionally large, fully double, intensely fragrant white flowers on a plant more compact and reliably cold-hardy than many older gardenia cultivars, making it a good fit for foundation plantings and smaller beds where a big gardenia bloom is still wanted. It flowers over a long season from late spring into summer, and its improved cold tolerance extends dependable gardenia culture a bit further north than older selections allow. Like all gardenias it is sensitive to soil pH, developing yellow, chlorotic leaves if the soil is not sufficiently acidic, so use an acid-forming fertilizer and keep soil consistently moist for the healthiest, most floriferous plant.

common_name: Four Seasons Gardenia (Reblooming Double White Gardenia)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic soil in partial shade; Four Seasons is a reblooming gardenia that flowers in a strong spring flush and then continues intermittently through summer and into fall.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade to morning sun with afternoon shade. Four Seasons lives up to its name among gardenia cultivars by reblooming intermittently through summer and into fall after its main spring flush, extending the fragrant, double white flowers well beyond the shorter bloom window of many older gardenia cultivars. The dense, glossy-leaved shrub makes a good foundation or specimen planting near a porch, window, or path where its strong fragrance can be enjoyed up close through multiple seasons. Like all gardenias it is sensitive to soil pH, developing yellow, chlorotic leaves in insufficiently acidic soil, so feed with acid-forming fertilizer and keep moisture consistent to support the extended bloom cycle.

common_name: Heaven Scent Gardenia (Exceptionally Fragrant Upright Gardenia)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic soil in partial shade; Heaven Scent is a Southern Living Plant Collection gardenia bred for especially strong fragrance on a compact, upright plant.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade to morning sun with afternoon shade, ideally near a patio, porch, or walkway where its fragrance can be fully appreciated. Heaven Scent is a Southern Living Plant Collection gardenia selected specifically for exceptionally strong, sweet fragrance, considered among the most powerfully scented gardenia cultivars available, carried on a compact, upright, well-branched shrub with glossy dark green foliage. Its manageable size fits foundation plantings and smaller beds better than some larger gardenia cultivars while still delivering an outsized fragrance impact. Like all gardenias it is sensitive to soil pH, developing yellow, chlorotic leaves in insufficiently acidic soil, so feed with acid-forming fertilizer and maintain consistent moisture for the healthiest, most fragrant bloom.

common_name: All Summer Beauty Hydrangea (Reliable Reblooming Mophead Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; All Summer Beauty is an older reblooming bigleaf hydrangea, flowering reliably on new wood even after a hard winter cuts back old stems.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, sheltered from hot afternoon sun and drying wind. All Summer Beauty is an older bigleaf hydrangea cultivar valued for setting flower buds reliably on new wood, so it continues to bloom through summer even in years when a late freeze damages old stems and buds, a problem that leaves many other mopheads bloomless for a season. Its large, rounded mophead flower clusters shift from blue to pink depending on soil pH, blue in acidic soil and pink in more alkaline soil, and can be nudged toward blue with aluminum sulfate or toward pink with garden lime. Water deeply during dry spells, since bigleaf hydrangea wilts readily in heat, and prune only lightly right after flowering to avoid removing next year's buds.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Hydrangea Species and Cultivars

common_name: Glowing Embers Hydrangea (Deep Pink-to-Purple German Mophead Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Glowing Embers is a longstanding German-bred mophead hydrangea still considered a top performer for deep, saturated flower color.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, sheltered from hot afternoon sun. Glowing Embers is a German-bred bigleaf hydrangea, roughly a half-century old, still regarded as one of the finest mopheads for deep, saturated flower color, ranging from rich pink in more alkaline soil to deep purple-red in strongly acidic soil, a shift managed with soil amendments if a specific shade is wanted. The large, rounded flower heads are held on a sturdy, well-branched, moderately compact shrub. Water deeply during dry spells to prevent wilting, and prune only lightly right after flowering, since flower buds for the following year form on the current season's growth by late summer.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Hydrangea Species and Cultivars

common_name: Little Quickfire Hydrangea (Compact Early-Blooming Panicle Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Little Quickfire is a compact sport of Quickfire panicle hydrangea, bred for a smaller mature size while keeping the same early-season white-to-pink bloom.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; panicle hydrangeas tolerate considerably more sun than bigleaf types. Little Quickfire is a compact sport of the popular Quickfire panicle hydrangea, offering the same trait of blooming several weeks earlier than most other panicle hydrangeas, with conical flower clusters opening white and aging to a rich pink-to-burgundy as the season progresses, but on a smaller-scale plant that fits foundation plantings and smaller beds where full-sized Quickfire would be too large. Unlike bigleaf hydrangeas, flower color is not affected by soil pH, and flower buds form on new wood, so it can be pruned back hard in late winter without sacrificing that year's bloom. Water deeply during dry spells and remove spent flower heads in late winter to tidy the plant before new growth begins.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Hydrangea Species and Cultivars

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; South Seas is an award-winning tetraploid daylily prized among collectors for its rich melon-coral color and heavy substance.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. South Seas is a tetraploid daylily bred by well-known hybridizer Curt Hanson, admired for its large, rich melon-to-coral-red flowers with a contrasting green throat and heavy, substantial petals that hold their color well through the heat of summer. Its award-winning bloom quality has made it a favorite among daylily collectors seeking strong, saturated warm colors distinct from the more common yellows and pastels. Like other daylilies it is easy to grow in average soil with routine watering, and mature clumps can be divided every three to four years in spring or fall to maintain vigor and increase the planting.

common_name: Ed Murray Daylily (Classic Near-Black Red Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Ed Murray, introduced in 1978, remains a benchmark near-black red daylily grown for its dark color and reliable rebloom.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Ed Murray, introduced in 1978, remains one of the most widely grown near-black red daylilies decades after its release, prized for its rich, deep red petals that read almost black in certain light, set off by a small chartreuse-green throat. Its dark, dramatic color and dependable, floriferous performance have kept it a benchmark against which other dark red daylilies are still measured. Like other daylilies it grows easily in average soil with routine watering, tolerates heat well, and mature clumps can be divided every three to four years in spring or fall to maintain vigor and increase the planting.

common_name: J.C. Harvey Crinum (Vigorous Pale Pink Pass-Along Crinum Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; J.C. Harvey is a Crinum moorei x zeylanicum hybrid known above all for extreme vigor and toughness, making it a classic Southern pass-along plant.

directions: Plant large bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, giving the plant room to form a substantial clump over time. J.C. Harvey is a hybrid crinum lily bearing large, pale pink, fragrant, trumpet-shaped flowers with darker reddish-pink buds atop tall stalks, but it is grown at least as much for its legendary vigor and toughness as for its bloom, having been passed hand to hand among Southern gardeners for generations as an almost indestructible landscape bulb. Established clumps tolerate drought, heat, and neglect once settled in, though they bloom best with regular moisture and feeding during the growing season. Crinums resent disturbance, so once planted, leave the clump undisturbed for years to reach full size and flowering potential, dividing only when significantly overcrowded.
